learningObjectives: Distinguish APIs, network services, XML, SOAP and REST.
Apply HTTP method semantics and scope SOAP method claims to the specified binding.
Separate an API representation format from an API Scan input format.
Configure and diagnose credentials using the service contract without assuming a universal token lifetime.

elements.description: An application programming interface defines how software components interact. It can be local or exposed through a network service; it is not necessarily a separate messenger program.
A service interface can be reached across a network. The HTTP examples here use request and response messages; the public World Wide Web is not required for every private network API.

elements.text: A mouse is a device that software can access through interfaces, not literally an application programming interface itself.

elements.description: SOAP defines a messaging framework; REST is an architectural style with constraints including a uniform interface and stateless interactions. Neither term means every endpoint implements every possible method.

rows: Retrieve a selected representation of the target resource.
Ask the resource to process the supplied representation according to its semantics; creation is one use.
Create or replace the target resource state with the supplied representation.
Request removal of the association between the target URI and its functionality.

elements.text: The SOAP 1.2 HTTP binding maps its request-response pattern to POST and its SOAP-response pattern to GET. Other bindings can differ; SOAP is not universally POST-only. Inspect the service binding and contract.

SOAP messaging uses an XML-based envelope model. REST representations are not restricted to one format; media types and the service contract determine accepted representations, such as XML, JSON or text.

elements.description: Extensible Markup Language represents document data and logical structure through markup. It can be used in messages or local files. Well-formed XML is not automatically valid against a schema or correct according to business rules.

Use an authorized sandbox with a published API contract. The historical DemoWebShop/Coffeeshop course mapping and training endpoint availability were not verified, so these notes do not require either service.

Configure credentials in the required location: the API Scan message section exposes authentication, parameters and headers separately. A query parameter named key and a 24-hour lifetime are not universal REST requirements.

elements.title: Diagnose a rejected credential
items: Inspect the actual status, response body and service documentation.
Check the intended environment, credential placement, permissions and validity period.
Check accidental whitespace without changing meaningful credential characters.
Obtain replacement credentials through the authorized workflow where required; do not publish them in shared notes or URLs.

examPitfalls.title: Treating SOAP as universally POST-only
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Generalizing a common request-response example to every SOAP binding.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: SOAP 1.2 HTTP maps request-response to POST and SOAP-response to GET; inspect the actual binding.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing representation and scan-input formats
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming an API Scan input list restricts every possible REST representation.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: REST can transfer different media types; the particular service contract controls accepted formats.

examPitfalls.title: Treating every API as a public web endpoint
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Ignoring local interfaces or private network services.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: APIs include local and network interfaces; the HTTP exercises are one network case.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming every REST token expires after 24 hours
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Applying an unverified training-service lifetime to all credentials.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use the actual service contract and credential metadata; authentication methods and validity periods vary.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In the SOAP 1.2 HTTP binding defined by W3C, which method corresponds to the request-response message exchange pattern?

options.text: GET
POST
Every HTTP method interchangeably
SOAP can never be carried over HTTP

practiceQuiz.hint: The question names a specific binding and exchange pattern.
practiceQuiz.rationale: This binding maps request-response to POST and SOAP-response to GET. It does not establish that every SOAP operation in every binding is POST-only.

optionExplanations.A: GET corresponds to the SOAP-response pattern in this binding.
optionExplanations.B: POST corresponds to the specified request-response pattern.
optionExplanations.C: The binding maps methods to particular patterns, not interchangeably.
optionExplanations.D: W3C defines the HTTP binding discussed here.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which representation formats can a REST service support, subject to its contract?

options.text: XML only
JSON only
Different media types, such as XML, JSON or text
REST cannot carry message content

practiceQuiz.hint: REST is an architectural style rather than a single serialization format.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Representations can use different data types. The specific API contract still determines which formats a particular operation accepts.

optionExplanations.A: REST does not require XML as its sole representation.
optionExplanations.B: JSON is common but not mandatory or exclusive.
optionExplanations.C: Different representations are possible; the endpoint contract governs support.
optionExplanations.D: REST interactions exchange representations, which can include content.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which statement about PUT matches HTTP semantics?

options.text: It is always read-only.
It can create or replace the target resource state using the supplied representation.
It only updates existing resources and can never create one.
It is only valid for SOAP.

practiceQuiz.hint: Distinguish creation at a known target from the processing semantics of POST.
practiceQuiz.rationale: RFC 9110 defines PUT as requesting creation or replacement of the target resource state; it is not limited to updating existing entries.

optionExplanations.A: PUT requests a state change rather than read-only retrieval.
optionExplanations.B: This includes both creation and replacement at the target resource.
optionExplanations.C: HTTP explicitly permits a successful PUT to create the target representation.
optionExplanations.D: PUT is an HTTP method and is not restricted to SOAP.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An API contract requires a credential in a particular header. How should the request be configured?

options.text: Omit the credential because all REST endpoints are public.
Use the required header and the credential validity rules specified by that service.
Always put it in a query parameter named key.
Assume every credential is permanent.

practiceQuiz.hint: Use the actual contract rather than a historical demo convention.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Credential location, authentication method and expiration are service-specific. API Scan exposes headers, authentication and parameters as distinct controls.

optionExplanations.A: The question explicitly specifies required credentials.
optionExplanations.B: The service contract determines correct placement and validity.
optionExplanations.C: A historical key parameter does not override the required header.
optionExplanations.D: Permanence is not established; follow the actual validity rules.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A service rejects a request containing a credential. Which diagnostic approach is appropriate?

options.text: API Scan cannot configure authentication.
Inspect the response and check environment, placement, permissions, expiry and accidental whitespace.
Credentials only work in a browser UI.
Credentials can never be used with POST.

practiceQuiz.hint: Several causes can produce rejection; avoid guessing a guaranteed single cause.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Check the response and service-specific requirements. Whitespace or expiry are possible causes, but neither is proven by rejection alone.

optionExplanations.A: The documented message section includes authentication configuration.
optionExplanations.B: These checks diagnose several plausible causes without asserting unverified frequencies or lifetimes.
optionExplanations.C: API clients can send credentials according to the service contract.
optionExplanations.D: Authentication is not categorically prohibited for POST.

quickRecap.value: A software interface can be local or exposed over a network.
SOAP is a messaging framework; REST is an architectural style.
W3C SOAP 1.2 HTTP request-response uses POST; SOAP-response uses GET. Inspect bindings.
POST requests resource-specific processing; PUT requests target-state creation or replacement.
Markup represents document data/structure; syntax alone does not prove schema or business correctness.
Use an authorized documented sandbox; historical course SUT mappings are unverified.
Placement, permissions and validity are service-specific; inspect actual rejection evidence.
